claim: Cohen, Malloy, Pomorski (2012, Journal of Finance 67(3):1009-1043) 'Decoding Inside Information' split Form 4 insider trades into 'routine' (same calendar month traded in each of the prior 3 years) vs 'opportunistic' (all others). US common stocks. Reported: value-weighted abnormal returns of 82 basis points per month from a portfolio of opportunistic-insider purchases; abnormal returns to routine-trader portfolios are essentially zero. Opportunistic sellers show significantly negative abnormal returns (their most-informed subgroup: nonexecutive insiders at small, geographically-concentrated, weak-governance firms). Separately, web search (not independently page-verified; SSRN and MDPI both returned HTTP 403 to direct fetch) surfaced a 2024-2025 replication using Form 4 data 2008-2024 reporting that the opportunistic-trade factor-adjusted alpha has decayed roughly 60-70%, from about 1.2-1.6%/month in the original sample window to about 0.3-0.4%/month in 2008-2024, with opportunistic-sell alpha now weak/insignificant versus the original -0.6%/month. This replication is very likely the same paper as the already-covered JEF 2025 'Insider trading and anomalies' (Tian, Xiang, Xu) rather than an independent update -- flagged, not counted as a second verified source.
impact_on_spec: Screen-library column: 'opportunistic_insider_flag' derived from Form 4 (SEC EDGAR, free) filer trade-timing history (routine = same-month trade in each of trailing 3 years). Feed as a monthly PIT feature packet (filing acceptance datetime is the point-in-time timestamp, not trade date) rather than a 1m cell; decay evidence means any promotion gate must re-measure current-sample alpha, not cite the 2012 number.
limitations: Original result is 1990s-2006 sample and monthly-rebalanced portfolio-level abnormal return, not a cross-sectional IC; not reproduced in-repo. The 2024-2025 decay figures come from web-search synthesis of SSRN/MDPI pages that WebFetch could not load (403), so those specific numbers are unverified secondhand and may duplicate the already-covered JEF 2025 source rather than add new evidence.

claim: Hong, Li, Ni, Scheinkman, Yan, 'Days to Cover and Stock Returns' (NBER Working Paper 21166, May 2015; JEL G12). US equities. Days-to-cover (DTC) = short ratio (shares shorted / shares outstanding) divided by average daily share turnover, i.e. the number of days needed for all shorts to cover given normal trading volume; approximates the arbitrageur's marginal shorting cost. Abstract's exact reported number: 'A long-short strategy using DTC generates a 1.2% monthly return,' and DTC is stated to be a better predictor of poor stock returns than the raw short-interest ratio. A companion web-search snippet (not directly page-verified; source not re-fetched) cited an equal-weighted DTC hedge return of 1.19%/month vs. 0.71%/month for short-interest-ratio over 1988-2012. Separately, a 2023 short-interest 'surprise' factor paper (Journal of Empirical Finance-style venue, ScienceDirect, S1386418123000393) was located reporting that a short-interest surprise measure remains predictive out-of-sample in international data and is not explained by standard risk factors or other short-selling proxies, but ScienceDirect returned HTTP 403 to direct fetch so its exact IC/return numbers are unverified here.
impact_on_spec: Screen-library column: 'days_to_cover' and 'short_interest_ratio' computed from FINRA biweekly short-interest files (free, ~2-week reporting lag) joined to a trailing average-daily-volume OHLCV field. PIT granularity is biweekly (settlement date + FINRA publish date), so this is a screen/rebalance-frequency column, not a 1m cell; usable as a monthly rank feature for a cross-sectional book, or as a slow gate/filter on a daily strategy's universe.
limitations: Core verified number (1.2%/month) is from a 2015 working paper never confirmed as peer-reviewed-published in this fetch, sample predates 2023-2026, and is a monthly-rebalanced long-short portfolio return, not a cross-sectional IC. FINRA short interest itself now has a material reporting lag relative to same-day OHLCV, and the 2023 'surprise' factor's exact current numbers could not be verified (ScienceDirect 403).

claim: Angelini, Iqbal, Jivraj, 'Systematic 13F Hedge Fund Alpha' (Barclays QIS / Novus, first version Oct 2019; published by Barclays same title). US-listed stocks, 13F filings from institutions holding >$100M (SEC EDGAR, free, filed within 45 days of quarter-end). Method: builds 'conviction' and 'consensus' measures across hedge-fund 13Fs (extending Cohen-Polk-Silli 2010's mutual-fund 'best ideas' test to hedge funds), and selects the subset of managers with longer-term views. Exact abstract text: 'a strategy that combines conviction and consensus of such managers... outperforms the S&P500 by 3.80% on average and delivers a Sharpe ratio of 0.75 over the period May 2004 to June 2019.' Search-only (unverified) supplementary color: a separate search snippet described a 'top high conviction positions' cut with six-factor alpha of 0.32%/month, and noted 2024-2025 hedge-fund 13F/crowding commentary (Goldman Sachs survey citing 5.8% 2025 quant-equity alpha; a 'crowding paradox' industry note) without a directly fetched primary page.
impact_on_spec: Screen-library column: quarterly 'hedge_fund_conviction_consensus_rank' built from free EDGAR 13F XML, joined to the equity universe with a 45-day-plus filing lag as the PIT timestamp (13F 'as of' quarter-end date must not be used as the visible_at date). Best used as a slow, quarterly-rebalanced screen/tilt column, not a timing gate or 1m cell.
limitations: Sample ends June 2019, five-plus years before this survey's 2024-2026 window; industry/Barclays-affiliated authors with a QIS commercial interest in the result; 13F excludes short positions and options, and the 45-day disclosure lag means the signal is materially stale versus the fund's actual current book. Six-factor alpha and crowding figures were not independently page-verified.

claim: Lou, Polk, Skouras, 'A tug of war: Overnight versus intraday expected returns' (Journal of Financial Economics 134 (2019) 192-213; NBER/SSRN circulated earlier). US stocks (large-cap-inclusive, robust ex small-cap). Exact published text: 'a portfolio that buys the value-weight overnight winner decile and sells the value-weight overnight loser decile has a three-factor overnight alpha of 3.47% per month with an associated t-statistic of 16.83 and a three-factor intraday alpha of -3.02% per month (t-statistic of -9.74).' Symmetric result for intraday momentum: intraday winner-minus-loser decile has a three-factor intraday alpha of 2.41%/month (t=7.70) and three-factor overnight alpha of -1.77%/month (t=-7.89). Patterns persist up to 60 months with joint-test t-stats over 20. 9 of 14 return-predicting strategies studied earn their entire premium intraday; 5 (past-return momentum variants and short-term reversal) earn it entirely overnight. Unverified (search-only, MDPI page returned HTTP 403 to fetch): a 2025/2026 MDPI International Journal of Financial Studies paper ('A Comparative Analysis of Overnight vs. Daytime Static and Momentum Strategies Across Sector ETFs') reportedly tests 10 US sector ETFs over 1999-2025 and finds overnight/reversal strategies outperform buy-and-hold before costs, with outperformance 'decreasing significantly' after transaction costs.
impact_on_spec: Direct fit for a 1-minute or daily-bar ETF cell: an 'overnight_vs_intraday_return' pair of PIT features (close-to-open, open-to-close) computable from free daily OHLCV with zero extra data cost, usable as a timing gate on execution style (hold overnight vs. flatten at close) for the momentum/reversal legs already in the repo's ETF router work.
limitations: Alphas are gross of transaction costs and pre-2019 sample; overnight returns are known to be sensitive to bid-ask bounce/close-open microstructure and to have compressed since wide retail adoption of extended-hours and 0DTE flows post-2020, which this paper does not cover. The one located 2024-2026 ETF-specific update could not be fetched (MDPI 403), so its exact numbers are unverified.

claim: Gao, Han, Li, Zhou, 'Market Intraday Momentum' (SSRN 2440866, current version June 2017; published Journal of Financial Economics 2018). SPY high-frequency data, 1993-2013 (also replicated on 10 other actively traded domestic/international ETFs). Finding: the first half-hour return since the prior close predicts the last half-hour return. Exact directly-read numbers: out-of-sample R^2_OS using the first half-hour return (r1) alone = 1.4%; using the twelfth half-hour return (r12) alone = 0.9%; using both combined = 2.0% (text: 'The R^2_OS's match or exceed those at the monthly frequency'). During the 2007-12-02 to 2009-06-30 financial crisis: r1 slope 13.6, R^2=4.1%; combined R^2=6.9%. Excluding crisis days: r1 R^2=0.8%, combined R^2=1.1%. Sorted by first-half-hour volatility tercile: low-vol R^2=0.6% (r1 coefficient insignificant), medium-vol R^2=1.0% (significant), high-vol R^2=3.3%. Predictability is weaker in the 7 days around month-end (T-3 to T+3) when institutional trading volume is about 5.9% lower. No explicit transaction-cost or net-of-cost strategy return table was found in the sections read (intro, out-of-sample, crisis, volatility/volume, liquidity, institutional trading, explanations); a dedicated profitability/cost section may exist elsewhere in the 48-page paper but was not located within this survey's budget, and no 2024-2026 follow-up with fresh numbers was searched for this item due to budget limits.
impact_on_spec: Directly a 1-minute/30-minute ETF cell candidate: on SPY/QQQ-type ETFs, a 'first_half_hour_return' PIT feature (computable live at 10:00am ET from free intraday bars) predicting the 3:30-4:00pm bar, conditioned on a volatility-tercile gate (R^2 is ~5.5x higher on high- vs low-volatility days) and a month-end-days exclusion filter.
limitations: R^2 values of 1-2% (up to ~7% only in the 2008 crisis subsample) are small and were not shown here net of transaction costs; a decile-spread / dollar P&L strategy return was not located in the pages read. Sample ends 2013, before the post-2015 rise of zero-commission retail flow, 0DTE options, and modern HFT market structure that could have eroded or altered this pattern; no 2024-2026 replication was checked for this item.

claim: Searched for 2024-2026 academic/quant evidence on (a) overnight gap fade/reversal in US stocks and (b) volatility-compression breakout (e.g. Bollinger/ATR squeeze). Found only retail trading-blog content (setup4alpha, TradeZella, SharePlanner, QuantifiedStrategies, TraderInsight, RizeTrade) and one QuantConnect community forum post ('Mind the Gap: An Intraday Reversal Strategy Using Gap Downs and ATR' -- rule: at the open, if a stock gaps down more than 1.2x its 14-day ATR vs. the prior close, go long and liquidate 15 minutes after the open). WebFetch of the QuantConnect thread confirmed the rule text but explicitly found no CAGR, Sharpe, win-rate, sample period, or universe reported in the visible thread (the linked external backtest was not itself fetched). Blog claims (unverified, no primary data): gaps within about +/-0.25% tend to fill same-day; gaps of 2%+ become case/news-specific; a +1% Monday gap-up is 'sold into'/gap-filled roughly 60% of the time. No IC, decile spread, or peer-reviewed 2024-2026 study with real numbers was located for either sub-direction within this survey's search budget.
impact_on_spec: Not ready to enter the repo as a screen column, packet, or 1m cell: no verified IC/return evidence exists yet. If pursued, treat as a hypothesis to test in-house on the repo's own OHLCV data (gap size as multiple of trailing ATR, next-bar/day return) rather than citing any external number as a promotion input.
limitations: This card documents an evidence gap, not a verified factor: every quantitative claim found is retail-blog-sourced with no disclosed sample, cost model, or statistical significance test. Do not use the 60% gap-fill figure or the 1.2x ATR rule as backtest inputs without independent, in-repo re-derivation.

claim: Irene Aldridge, 'Liquidity Premium and Investment Horizons' (arXiv 2607.01377v1, econ.EM, posted 1 Jul 2026). Entire CRSP US equity universe, daily and monthly data, 2020-2025. Constructs firm-month signed order flow and two Kyle (1985) lambda estimators from daily price/volume data only (no tick data): Method A = Amihud-style ratio (mean |return|/dollar volume); Method B = within-month regression slope of price change on signed volume. Exact reported numbers: Table 9 Fama-MacBeth cross-sectional regressions of next-month returns on the lambda signal give mean slope beta=-0.0122 (t[NW]=-2.27**) for the Amihud-style lambda and beta=-0.0050 (t[NW]=-2.25**) over T=58 months (mean intercept ~0.0130-0.0132, t~1.65-1.68*). Table 6/8 pooled return regressions on lambda_it directly: coefficients of -101.2*** (t=-6.46) and 1355*** (t=4.08) depending on specification, but pooled R^2 is only 0.0000-0.0001 across all four specifications (N~438,465-438,471 firm-months) -- i.e., statistically significant but explains essentially none of the variance. Paper's own framing: 'order-flow based measures... carry reliable, if modest, cross-sectional information about future returns.'
impact_on_spec: Screen-library column: a monthly 'signed_order_flow_lambda' feature computable entirely from free daily OHLCV+volume (Amihud-style ratio needs only |return| and dollar volume; the regression-based estimator needs within-month daily price/volume pairs), no tick or order-book data required. Fits as a slow cross-sectional tilt/rank column alongside existing screen factors, not a 1m cell or timing gate -- the R^2~0 result means it should not be a standalone signal.
limitations: Very small explanatory power (pooled R^2 essentially 0 despite significant t-stats); only T=58 months in the Fama-MacBeth panel; single-author, very recent (Jul 2026) arXiv preprint, not yet peer reviewed; author (Irene Aldridge) is an industry practitioner-academic with a commercial HFT/liquidity research background, a possible conflict of interest to note. No decile-spread trading strategy return or realistic cost/capacity analysis is given.

claim: Web-search synthesis (primary pages not successfully fetched: ACM DL returned HTTP 403) surfaced: (1) Ni, Liu et al.-style ACM paper 'Highly Regarded Investors? Mining Predictive Value from the Collective Intelligence of Reddit's WallStreetBets' (ACM, 2024 conference proceedings, doi 10.1145/3614419.3643993) -- claimed to mine predictive value from WSB collective intelligence but exact IC/return numbers not independently confirmed. (2) A PMC-indexed paper 'Financial recommendations on Reddit, stock returns and cumulative prospect theory' finding WSB posting volume does NOT predict next-month alpha, but WSB *sentiment* does, acting as a CONTRARIAN indicator: more-positive-sentiment stocks tend to underperform next month and more-negative-sentiment stocks tend to outperform (direction only; no effect size independently confirmed). (3) A non-academic blog (fffinstill.com) claims to have back-tested 4,483 Reddit mention signals against 5-day forward returns across 10 finance subreddits, but was not fetched. (4) A 2024 ScienceDirect paper 'Dumb money? Social network attention herding, sentiment, and markets' reports an event-study pattern of positive-sentiment stocks' buy-and-hold abnormal returns rising into peak WSB attention (pump) -- consistent with attention-driven overreaction/reversal, no numbers confirmed. No IC, decile spread, or Sharpe number from any of these was verified by direct page read.
impact_on_spec: If pursued: a weekly/daily PIT feature packet from free Google Trends (public API, ~1-3 day lag, weekly-normalized index only, no raw counts) and free-tier Reddit/Pushshift-style mention counts (access to Reddit's API has tightened materially and is no longer reliably free at scale -- a real data-access limit). Best framed as a contrarian sentiment-extreme gate/filter rather than a standalone screen column, given the reversal direction reported above.
limitations: No claim in this card has a directly page-verified effect size; several sources (ACM, ScienceDirect) were blocked (403) and one source is a non-peer-reviewed blog. Google Trends access is free but rate-limited and only relative/normalized; Reddit's API has moved away from free bulk access since 2023, which is a material feasibility constraint for a single person, not just an alpha question.

claim: Web-search synthesis (primary pages not fetched; this survey's 25-call budget was exhausted before a direct fetch could be made) on two well-known papers. (1) Lopez-Lira & Tang, 'Can ChatGPT Forecast Stock Price Movements? Return Predictability and Large Language Models' (arXiv 2304.07619; SSRN 4412788). Method: feed daily news headlines to GPT-4/ChatGPT, score sentiment, form long-short portfolios. Reported (per search synthesis, not page-verified): using post-training-cutoff headlines, GPT-4 achieves 'approximately 90% portfolio-day hit rates for the non-tradable initial reaction,' and GPT-4 scores 'significantly predict the subsequent drift, especially for small stocks and negative news'; forecasting ability increases with model size. (2) Kim, Muhn, Nikolaev, 'Bloated Disclosures: Can ChatGPT Help Investors Process Information?' (arXiv 2306.10224). Method: have ChatGPT summarize 10-K/10-Q MD&A and earnings-call text (free EDGAR source text) into shorter, more sentiment-pronounced summaries; reported (per search synthesis) that the ChatGPT-refined summaries have 'more significant explanatory power over the abnormal returns surrounding the disclosure days than the original texts.' Neither paper's exact Sharpe ratio, IC, or decile-spread numbers were confirmed by direct page read in this survey.
impact_on_spec: If confirmed: an LLM-derived, point-in-time news/filing sentiment feature packet (per this repo's existing PIT-packet requirement for LLM/news inputs) built from free EDGAR full-text search API (10-K/10-Q/8-K) plus a cheap LLM call per filing; the headline-based Lopez-Lira/Tang design needs a free-or-cheap news-headline feed, which is the binding data-cost constraint, not the LLM call itself.
limitations: Not independently verified in this pass -- both citations rest on search-engine summarization, not a primary-source read, because the 25-web-call budget for this survey was exhausted on higher-priority items first. Known general risks for this literature (from prior repo research already covered, e.g. AlphaMemo's Alpha158 decay finding) apply: reported LLM-alpha numbers are frequently in-sample/backtested on the same headline corpus used for prompt design, and GPT-4-era numbers may not replicate with cheaper/current models.

claim: Explicit search for a 2025-2026 paper reporting cross-sectional IC above 0.05 on US equities with OHLCV-only inputs. This was the final search this survey's 25-call budget allowed, so it is search-synthesis-only (no primary page fetched/read). Two candidates surfaced, NEITHER clearly satisfies 'OHLCV-only': (1) A 2026 arXiv paper (title/authors not resolved in the snippet) reports a 'Risk-Regime IC' that 'rose to 0.0515 (p<0.0001)' on a 2025 holdout period, described as confirming 'signal persistence out-of-sample' -- the underlying feature construction (whether OHLCV-derived regime detection or something else) was not confirmed. (2) A separate 2026 paper on LLM-derived trading features (arXiv 2604.10996, 'When Valid Signals Fail: Regime Boundaries Between LLM Features and RL Trading Policies,' appeared in the same search) reports, per the search synthesis, that a 'conflicting_signals' feature achieved IC=0.233 and an 'impact' feature achieved IC=0.177 -- both far above 0.05, but these are explicitly LLM-derived features, not OHLCV-only, so they do not answer this item's question; they are recorded here only as context that IC>0.05 is achievable with richer inputs. No paper was found and confirmed in this pass reporting IC>0.05 on a clearly OHLCV-only US equity cross-section.
impact_on_spec: No direct spec impact yet -- this is an open question, not a verified factor. If a genuine OHLCV-only IC>0.05 source is found in a follow-up pass, it would be high-value as a screen-library column since it requires no paid data; until then this repo should treat 'IC>0.05 from OHLCV alone' as a hypothesis to test in-house (e.g. against the already-covered Alpha158/Alpha101/Alpha191 baselines) rather than an established external benchmark to match.
limitations: Fully unverified: found via a single search query at the very end of a budget-exhausted survey, no primary source fetched, and the two candidate numbers found are either of unclear feature construction (Risk-Regime IC) or explicitly not OHLCV-only (the LLM-feature ICs). Should not be cited as evidence that an OHLCV-only IC>0.05 signal exists or does not exist on 2025-2026 US equities; needs a dedicated follow-up search.
